newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark pledges to slash state debt by year 2005.
newsitem.headline: Denmark pledges to slash state debt by year 2005.

text.p: Denmark's government pledged on Wednesday to slash state debt by the year 2005 to 40 percent of Gross Domestic Product, from its present level of 70 percent.
A government statement announcing economic plans for the coming eight years also forecast average unemployment of 5.0 percent in 2005, compared to 8.8 percent in 1996.
It also saw 1997 GDP growth at 2.8 percent, up from 2.4 percent in 1996. Average annual GDP growth in the years 1998 to 2005 was seen at 2.3 percent.

The debt forecast was in line with a previous government prediction but the 1997 GDP growth prognosis was a downward revision from a previous estimate of 3.1 percent and the 2005 unemployment forecast was down from a previous 5.6 percent.
Government data shows 1996 state debt at 706 billion crowns, of which 321 billion crowns -- 32 percent of GDP -- was foreign borrowing.
Presenting the proposals, Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen said that his debt reduction plan left little room to reduce taxes although there would be gradual cuts over the eight-year period.
Denmark's standard rate of income tax is currently 51.8 percent.
"As we are so ambitious regarding debt we cannot promise large tax cuts," he said, adding that another priority was to keep wage rises modest and encourage job creation.
"That is an offer to which the opposition will find it hard to say "no", this is an invitation to collaborate," Rasmussen said.
Denmark's annual budget, to be presented in draft form in August, is traditionally passed by consensus between the government, historically a minority, and opposition parties.

In a break with tradition, the main opposition Liberal and Conservatives refused to support the 1997 budget, leaving Rasmussen's Social Democrat-led coalition dependent on the far left to get the bill through parliament.
General elections are to be held by September 1998 and polls point to a centre-right coalition ousting the present government. --Steve Weizman, Copenhagen newsroom +45 33 9696560
